Pass the key to the rows; send "activate" for an activate command they leave unhandled.

Returns:

None if the rows or an "activate" handler handled the key, otherwise the key. A handler handles the key by returning a true value.

property layout: TableLayout¶

The layout of the columns, which builds and measures the rows.

property max_rows: int | None¶

The most rows of body a flow size shows; None shows every row.

mouse_event(size: tuple[()] | tuple[int] | tuple[int, int], event: str, button: int, col: int, row: int, focus: bool) → bool | None¶

Pass the event to the rows; the header and the footer take no mouse events.

pack(size: tuple[()] | tuple[int] | tuple[int, int] = (), focus: bool = False) → tuple[int, int]¶

Return the natural width and the rows at it for (), as Widget.pack() does otherwise.

render(size: tuple[()] | tuple[int] | tuple[int, int], focus: bool = False) → Canvas¶

Render the header, the rows and the footer, top to bottom.

property row_attr: Callable[[int, Any], _AttrMapLike | None] | None¶

row_attr(index, data), called each time a row renders, or None.

A result other than None is the row’s attribute map, in any form AttrMap takes, over TableRow.attr. A focused row with a focus map uses that instead. A change of the rows calls it again for the rows from the changed position on; a data object changed in place is seen only when the row is assigned again (body[i] = body[i]).

rows(size: tuple[int], focus: bool = False) → int¶

Return the header, body and footer rows, at most max_rows of body.

Without max_rows every row is measured.

selectable() → bool¶

Return whether the table has a row to focus.

set_focus(position: int, coming_from: Literal['above', 'below'] | None = None) → None¶

Focus the row at position, as ListBox.set_focus() does.

A row on screen from the old focus is brought just into view. Without coming_from:

  • a row on screen keeps its cursor and nested focus;

  • a row off screen is centred and keeps its nested focus.

With coming_from:

  • a row on screen takes the cursor from that edge, at the preferred column;

  • a row off screen is placed at that edge and keeps its nested focus.

Parameters:

  • position – the index of the row

  • coming_from – "above" or "below" when the old focus is on that side of the new one

Raises:

  • IndexError – position is not an index of a row.

  • ListBoxError – coming_from is not "above", "below" or None.

Return BOX and FLOW, and FIXED as well when no column is weighted.

Attribute map applied to the focused row while the table renders without focus, see ListBox.

TableRow¶

class urwid.TableRow(layout: TableLayout, cells: Sequence[_Cell], *, data: Any = None, attr: _AttrMapLike | None = None, focus_attr: _AttrMapLike | None = None, selectable: bool = True, span: bool = False)¶

One row of cells laid out by a TableLayout.

A row is selectable unless built with selectable=False, whatever its cells, so a row of plain text can take the focus in a Table.

The attribute map applied to the row’s canvas is, in this order:

  • focus_attr, or the table’s focus_attr, when the row renders in focus;

  • the result of the table’s row_attr callable, when it returns something other than None;

  • attr, or the table’s attr.

The attr of a TableColumn maps each cell of that column first, except in a span row, in the header of a Table and in a footer the table built from cells. A row map given as a dict then also maps the cells’ and the columns’ attributes. The attribute a row map gives for None becomes the base layer under them.

Build the row and register it with layout.

Parameters:

  • layout – the layout whose widths the row uses

  • cells – one widget or text markup per column; a short row is padded with empty text cells. Text markup becomes a text cell with the column’s align and wrap. The sequence is copied.

  • data – any object the caller keeps with the row, such as the record it shows

  • attr – attribute map of the row, in any form AttrMap takes

  • focus_attr – attribute map of the row while it renders in focus

  • selectable – whether the row takes the focus

TableColumn¶

class urwid.TableColumn(label: _TagMarkup = '', width: Literal[WHSettings.PACK] | int | tuple[Literal[WHSettings.WEIGHT], int | float] = WHSettings.PACK, min_width: int = 1, align: Literal[Align.LEFT, Align.CENTER, Align.RIGHT] = Align.LEFT, wrap: Literal[WrapMode.SPACE, WrapMode.CLIP, WrapMode.ELLIPSIS] = WrapMode.CLIP, attr: _AttrMapLike | None = None)¶

Specification of one table column.

The width is one of:

  • WHSettings.PACK: as wide as the widest cell that can be measured, and the label;

  • a number of screen columns, where 0 hides the column;

  • (WHSettings.WEIGHT, weight): a share of the room left by the other columns.

align and wrap apply to the cells given as text; a cell given as a widget keeps its own. attr maps every cell of the column; TableRow gives the order in which it and the row maps apply. A TableLayout validates the specification when it takes it.

Create new instance of TableColumn(label, width, min_width, align, wrap, attr)

align: Literal[Align.LEFT, Align.CENTER, Align.RIGHT]¶

Alias for field number 3

attr: _AttrMapLike | None¶

Attribute map of the column’s cells; the header label, a footer built from cells and a span row do not use it.

label: _TagMarkup¶

Header text, drawn by Table with header=True.

min_width: int¶

The narrowest a PACK or WEIGHT column becomes before the table hides a column instead.

width: Literal[WHSettings.PACK] | int | tuple[Literal[WHSettings.WEIGHT], int | float]¶

Alias for field number 1

wrap: Literal[WrapMode.SPACE, WrapMode.CLIP, WrapMode.ELLIPSIS]¶

Alias for field number 4

TableLayout¶

class urwid.widget.TableLayout(columns: Sequence[TableColumn], *, dividechars: int = 1)¶

Column widths shared by every row built through the layout, with or without a Table.

Cells are measured once, when their row is built. A text cell the layout made measures itself again when its text changes. Another widget whose width changed needs invalidate_widths().

>>> from urwid import Pile
>>> layout = TableLayout([TableColumn(), TableColumn(align="right")])
>>> pile = Pile([layout.row(["name", "1"]), layout.row(["n", "22"])])
>>> [line.decode() for line in pile.render((10,)).text]
['name  1   ', 'n    22   ']

Validate the column specifications.

Parameters:

  • columns – one specification per column

  • dividechars – blank screen columns between two visible columns

Raises:

TableError – a specification or dividechars is invalid; the message names the column index.

property columns: tuple[TableColumn, ...]¶

The column specifications.

property dividechars: int¶

Blank screen columns between two visible columns.

invalidate_widths() → None¶

Measure every cell of every registered row again.

Call it after a cell widget given by the caller changed its packed width. Text cells the layout made from text markup do not need it.

natural_width() → int¶

Return the smallest width at which no column shrinks or is hidden.

It is the sum of the natural widths of the visible columns and their dividers, where a weighted column counts at its minimum.

row(cells: Sequence[_Cell], *, data: Any = None, attr: _AttrMapLike | None = None, focus_attr: _AttrMapLike | None = None, selectable: bool = True, span: bool = False) → TableRow¶

Build a row of this layout; see TableRow for the arguments.

Raises:

TableError – the row does not fit the columns, see TableRow.

widths(maxcol: int) → tuple[int, ...]¶

Return the width of each column at maxcol screen columns.

The widths and a divider between every two visible columns fit in maxcol. A width of 0 hides the column. When the natural widths do not fit, the weighted columns are at their minimum first, then the PACK columns shrink in proportion to how far they are above their minimum, and as the last resort the rightmost visible column is hidden. A given width never shrinks.

Raises:

TableError – maxcol is negative.

Tabs¶

class urwid.Tabs(tabs: Iterable[tuple[_TagMarkup | AbstractWidget, AbstractWidget]] = (), *, selected: int = 0, bar_position: Literal['top', 'bottom'] | VAlign = VAlign.TOP, bar_selectable: bool = False, attr_map: _AttrMapLike | None = None, selected_map: _AttrMapLike | None = None, focus_map: _AttrMapLike | None = None, unfocused_focus_attr: _AttrMapLike | None = None, unfocused_focus_attr_func: _UnfocusedFocusAttrFunc | None = None, dividechars: int = 1, overflow_markers: tuple[str, str] | None = (TabsSymbols.ARROW_ASCII_LEFT, TabsSymbols.ARROW_ASCII_RIGHT), underline: tuple[str, str] | None = None)¶

A row of tab labels over (or under) the body of the selected tab.

The selected tab is the focus of the container: focus_position is its index and focus its body. Only the selected body is rendered, and keys go to it. A button 1 press on a label selects its tab. The 'next tab' and 'previous tab' commands select the neighbour, wrapping around at the ends; no key is mapped to them by default, see CommandMap.

With bar_selectable=True the label row can take the keyboard focus: the command towards the bar ('cursor up' for a top bar), unhandled by the body, moves the focus to it. There 'cursor left' and 'cursor right' move a bar cursor without selecting, 'activate' selects the tab under it, and the command towards the body returns the focus there. focus_position stays the selected tab while the bar has the keyboard focus, so get_focus_widgets() names the body then. With a single tab there is nothing to switch to: the bar does not take the focus and the tab commands are returned.

Labels are display-only: each one is rendered as a fixed widget, trimmed to one row, and never gets input, so a label should have text. When the labels do not fit, the bar shows the selected label (the label under the bar cursor while the bar has the focus) centred, or its first column when it is wider than the bar. Each edge with labels hidden past it shows a marker of overflow_markers, and a click on it selects the nearest hidden tab on that side.

With underline set, a line row between the labels and the body draws its first glyph across the width and its second one along the selected label, which joins that label to its body. The line takes attr_map, and its part along the selected label selected_map. A click on the line acts as a click on the label row next to it, an overflow marker included.

Sends "focus changed" after focus_position changed, also through a change of contents. Its handlers receive the container, the old and the new index, which is None while it is empty. It reports the index, not the body: deleting the selected tab when another one follows it keeps the index, so the next tab becomes selected without a signal. An application that follows the selected body compares focus before and after its own contents changes.

>>> tabs = Tabs([("Log", Text("log body")), ("Edit", Text("edit body"))])
>>> tabs.render((12,)).text
[b'Log Edit    ', b'log body    ']
>>> tabs.focus_position = 1
>>> tabs.render((12,)).text
[b'Log Edit    ', b'edit body   ']

Build the tabs from (label, body) pairs.

Parameters:

  • tabs – one (label, body) pair per tab, in order. A label is a widget, or markup made into a widget by options().

  • selected – index of the tab selected first; ignored when tabs is empty.

  • bar_position – 'top' or 'bottom', where the label row is drawn.

  • bar_selectable – let the label row take the keyboard focus when there are two or more tabs.

  • attr_map – attribute map applied to every label, in any form AttrMap takes.

  • selected_map – attribute map applied to the label of the selected tab instead of attr_map.

  • focus_map – attribute map applied to the label under the bar cursor while the bar has the focus, instead of the other two.

  • unfocused_focus_attr – attribute map applied over the selected label while the tabs render without focus; see unfocused_focus_attr.

  • unfocused_focus_attr_func – function that gives the map applied over the selected label while the tabs render without focus, instead of unfocused_focus_attr; it is called with the selected label, see unfocused_focus_attr_func.

  • dividechars – blank screen columns between two labels.

  • overflow_markers – text drawn at the left and the right edge of the label row while labels are hidden past that edge, such as (Tabs.Symbols.ARROW_TRIANGLE_LEFT, Tabs.Symbols.ARROW_TRIANGLE_RIGHT); None draws none, and an empty string draws none on that side.

  • underline – the glyphs of a line row between the labels and the body: the one drawn across the width and the one drawn along the selected label, such as (Tabs.Symbols.LINE_LIGHT, Tabs.Symbols.LINE_HEAVY); None draws no line.

Raises:

  • TypeError – a body is not a widget.

  • TagMarkupException – a label is neither a widget nor valid text markup.

  • AttrMapError – a key or value of attr_map, selected_map, focus_map or unfocused_focus_attr is not hashable.

  • ValueError – a label is not a fixed widget, a body is neither a flow nor a box widget, bar_position is not 'top' or 'bottom', dividechars is not an int >= 0, overflow_markers is not None or a pair of one-line strings, or underline is not None or a pair of one-column strings.

  • IndexError – selected is not an index of tabs.

keypress(size: tuple[()] | tuple[int] | tuple[int, int], key: str) → str | None¶

Pass the key to the selected body, or to the bar while it has the focus.

A body with no rows shown gets no keys. The tab commands switch tabs when neither the bar nor the body used the key. “Towards the bar” is 'cursor up' for a top bar and 'cursor down' for a bottom bar.

no tabs -> return key
bar focused?
+- yes: left/right -> move the bar cursor; at an edge return key
|       activate -> select the tab under the bar cursor
|       towards the body, body selectable and shown -> focus the body
|       anything else -> tab commands below
+- no:  body selectable and shown -> body.keypress(); handled -> done
        towards the bar and the bar can take the focus -> focus the bar on the selected tab
        anything else -> tab commands below
tab commands, two or more tabs -> select the neighbour, wrapping around
otherwise -> return key
Raises:

TabsError – size is (), or a flow size and the selected body is not a flow widget.

mouse_event(size: tuple[()] | tuple[int] | tuple[int, int], event: str, button: int, col: int, row: int, focus: bool) → bool | None¶

Handle a mouse event on the bar or on the body.

A button 1 press on a label, or on the line next to it, selects its tab, and events on the body rows go to the body.

With a selectable bar the press also moves the keyboard focus to the bar. A press on the body while the bar has the focus returns the focus to the body.

Raises:

TabsError – size is (), or a flow size and the selected body is not a flow widget.

class urwid.widget.tabs.TabsSymbols(*values)¶

Common symbols for Tabs: overflow markers in left and right pairs, and underline glyphs.

The ARROW_ and GUILLEMET_ members are overflow markers, the LINE_ members underline glyphs. Only the ASCII members are also drawn on terminals without UTF-8, where the others are drawn as ?.

Note

The default terminal fonts of GNOME, KDE Plasma and Xfce on Ubuntu, Fedora and Arch, and of Windows Terminal, show every member. The default fonts of the Linux virtual console are:

  • Ubuntu: Fixed 8x16.

  • Fedora and openSUSE: eurlatgr.

  • Arch: the built-in 8x16 font of the kernel.

Overlay¶

class urwid.Overlay(top_w: TopWidget, bottom_w: BottomWidget, align: Literal['left', 'center', 'right'] | Align | tuple[Literal['relative', 'fixed left', 'fixed right', WHSettings.RELATIVE], int], width: Literal['pack', WHSettings.PACK] | int | tuple[Literal['relative', WHSettings.RELATIVE], int] | None, valign: Literal['top', 'middle', 'bottom'] | VAlign | tuple[Literal['relative', 'fixed top', 'fixed bottom', WHSettings.RELATIVE], int], height: Literal['pack', WHSettings.PACK] | int | tuple[Literal['relative', WHSettings.RELATIVE], int] | None, min_width: int | None = None, min_height: int | None = None, left: int = 0, right: int = 0, top: int = 0, bottom: int = 0, *, shrink_to_fit: bool = False)¶

Overlay contains two widgets and renders one on top of the other.

Top widget can be Box, Flow or Fixed. Bottom widget should be Box.

Sends "menu" when the top widget leaves a key for the menu command (esc by default) unhandled. Its handlers receive the overlay. A handler returning True consumes the key. Otherwise keypress() returns the key, as it does without a handler.

Sends "click outside" on a press of mouse button 1, 2 or 3 outside the top widget. Its handlers receive the overlay. A handler returning True consumes the press. Otherwise mouse_event() leaves the press unhandled, as it does without a handler.

Build the widget overlaying top_w on bottom_w.

Parameters:

  • top_w – a flow, box or fixed widget to overlay “on top”.

  • bottom_w – a box widget to appear “below” previous widget.

  • align – alignment, one of 'left', 'center', 'right' or ('relative', percentage 0=left 100=right)

  • width –

    width type, one of:

    'pack'

    if top_w is a fixed widget

    given width

    integer number of columns wide

    ('relative', percentage of total width)

    make top_w width related to container width

  • valign – alignment mode, one of 'top', 'middle', 'bottom' or ('relative', percentage 0=top 100=bottom)

  • height –

    one of:

    'pack'

    if top_w is a flow or fixed widget

    given height

    integer number of rows high

    ('relative', percentage of total height)

    make top_w height related to container height

  • min_width – the minimum number of columns for top_w when width is not fixed.

  • min_height – minimum number of rows for top_w when height is not fixed.

  • left – a fixed number of columns to add on the left.

  • right – a fixed number of columns to add on the right.

  • top – a fixed number of rows to add on the top.

  • bottom – a fixed number of rows to add on the bottom.

  • shrink_to_fit – with a 'pack' height, render a top_w taller than the rows available as a box at those rows, instead of cutting it off at the bottom. It applies only to a top_w that also supports 'box', such as a LineBox around a Table. It has no effect for other heights or for a 'pack' width.

Overlay widgets behave similarly to Padding and Filler widgets when determining the size and position of top_w. bottom_w is always rendered the full size available “below” top_w.

Deprecated since version 2.4.0: Passing a top_w or bottom_w that does not implement the Widget API is deprecated. Support will be removed in version 7.0.

property contents: MutableSequence[tuple[TopWidget | BottomWidget, OverlayOptions]]¶

A list-like object holding the overlay’s widgets and their options.

It is similar to:

[(bottom_w, bottom_options)),
 (top_w, top_options)]

This object may be used to read or update top and bottom widgets and top widgets’s options, but no widgets may be added or removed.

top_options takes the form (align_type, align_amount, width_type, width_amount, min_width, left, right, valign_type, valign_amount, height_type, height_amount, min_height, top, bottom)

bottom_options is always (‘left’, None, ‘relative’, 100, None, 0, 0, ‘top’, None, ‘relative’, 100, None, 0, 0) which means that bottom widget always covers the full area of the Overlay. writing a different value for bottom_options raises an OverlayError.

Returns:

Sizing information depends on the top widget sizing and sizing parameters.

Rules: * BOX sizing is always supported provided by the bottom widget * FLOW sizing is supported if top widget has: * * PACK height type and FLOW supported by the TOP widget * * BOX supported by TOP widget AND height amount AND height type GIVEN of min_height * FIXED sizing is supported if top widget has: * * PACK width type and FIXED supported by the TOP widget * * width amount and GIVEN width or min_width AND: * * * FLOW supported by the TOP widget AND PACK height type * * * BOX supported by the TOP widget AND height_amount and GIVEN height or min height

Warns OverlayWarning:

the top widget does not support the sizing its width or height type needs.

top¶

Number of rows of padding above the top widget.

property top_w: TopWidget¶

Widget overlaid “on top” of bottom_w.

top_w_size(size: tuple[int, int], left: int, right: int, top: int, bottom: int) → tuple[()] | tuple[int] | tuple[int, int]¶

Return the size to pass to top_w.

A 'pack' height gives a flow size. With shrink_to_fit it gives a box size of the rows between the fillers instead, when the top widget is taller than those rows in or out of focus.

property valign: VAlign | tuple[Literal[WHSettings.RELATIVE], int]¶

Return the simplified vertical alignment of the top widget.

property width: Literal[WHSettings.CLIP, WHSettings.PACK] | int | tuple[Literal[WHSettings.RELATIVE], int] | tuple[Literal[WHSettings.WEIGHT], int | float]¶

Return the simplified width of the top widget.

OverlayStack¶

class urwid.OverlayStack(base: Widget, *, close_on_menu: bool = False, close_on_click_outside: bool = False)¶

A box widget showing dialogs on top of a base widget.

Each dialog is an Overlay over the one below. open() puts a widget on top and close() takes it down again with a result. Only the top dialog receives keys and mouse presses. The widgets below keep their own focus, so closing a dialog returns the input to where it was. The stack adds no frame: wrap a dialog in a LineBox or an AttrMap before opening it.

The base is a box widget, usually the application’s Frame, and the stack is meant to be the MainLoop.widget.

Sends "closed" once per closed dialog, after the dialog is removed and after its on_close callback. Its handlers receive the stack, the widget that was closed and the result.

Important

Call every method from the thread running the loop, like every other widget change. Another thread hands the call over with MainLoop.call_from_thread().

>>> from urwid import SolidFill, Text
>>> stack = OverlayStack(SolidFill("."))
>>> stack.open(Text("hi"))
>>> stack.render((10, 3)).text
[b'..........', b'.hi      .', b'..........']
>>> stack.close()
True
>>> stack.close()
False

Build a stack with no dialog open.

Parameters:

  • base – box widget shown under every dialog, see base.

  • close_on_menu – default of open()’s close_on_menu, see close_on_menu.

  • close_on_click_outside – default of open()’s close_on_click_outside, see close_on_click_outside.

property base: Widget¶

The box widget shown under every dialog.

Setting it replaces the widget under the lowest dialog and keeps the dialogs open.

close(result: Any = None, *, widget: Widget | None = None) → bool¶

Close the top dialog, or widget and every dialog above it.

Each dialog above widget is closed first, the top one first, with the result None. Per dialog, in order: it is removed, its on_close is called, and "closed" is sent. A callback may therefore open or close dialogs itself.

widget given and not open, or nothing open -> return False
loop:
    remove the top dialog, show the one below
    on_close(result if it is widget else None), then "closed"
    it was widget, or a callback closed widget -> return True
    otherwise (widget still open, maybe under dialogs a callback opened) -> loop
Parameters:

  • result – passed to on_close and to the "closed" handlers of the dialog closed last.

  • widget – the dialog to close, as passed to open(). None closes the top dialog.

Returns:

whether a dialog was closed. It is False when no dialog is open, or when widget is not open in this stack.

property close_on_click_outside: bool¶

Whether a dialog opened from now on closes on a press of mouse button 1, 2 or 3 outside it.

The press closes the dialog only, and does not reach the widget under it. A change does not affect the dialogs already open.

property close_on_menu: bool¶

Whether a dialog opened from now on closes on a key for the menu command (esc by default).

The key closes the dialog only when the dialog leaves it unhandled. A change does not affect the dialogs already open.

property depth: int¶

The number of open dialogs.

property levels: tuple[Widget, ...]¶

The widgets of the open dialogs, as passed to open(), the lowest first.

open(widget: Widget, *, align: Literal['left', 'center', 'right'] | Align | tuple[Literal['relative', 'fixed left', 'fixed right', WHSettings.RELATIVE], int] = Align.CENTER, width: _Width | None = None, valign: Literal['top', 'middle', 'bottom'] | VAlign | tuple[Literal['relative', 'fixed top', 'fixed bottom', WHSettings.RELATIVE], int] = VAlign.MIDDLE, height: _Width | None = None, min_width: int | None = None, min_height: int | None = None, left: int = 0, right: int = 0, top: int = 0, bottom: int = 0, shrink_to_fit: bool = False, close_on_menu: bool | None = None, close_on_click_outside: bool | None = None, on_close: Callable[[Any], object] | None = None) → None¶

Open widget as a dialog on top of the stack.

The layout options are those of Overlay, and are passed to it unchanged. A width or height of None is chosen from widget.sizing():

  • width is "pack" for a widget that is fixed only, and ("relative", 80) otherwise.

  • height is "pack" for a flow widget, ("relative", 80) for a box widget that is not a flow widget, and "pack" for a widget that is fixed only.

Nothing is opened when an exception is raised.

Parameters:

  • widget – the dialog, a box, flow or fixed widget.

  • align – horizontal alignment, as for Overlay.

  • width – width, as for Overlay, or None to choose it from the sizing.

  • valign – vertical alignment, as for Overlay.

  • height – height, as for Overlay, or None to choose it from the sizing.

  • min_width – minimum number of columns for a relative width.

  • min_height – minimum number of rows for a relative height.

  • left – columns of padding on the left of the dialog.

  • right – columns of padding on the right of the dialog.

  • top – rows of padding above the dialog.

  • bottom – rows of padding below the dialog.

  • shrink_to_fit – with a "pack" height, render a dialog that also supports "box" and is taller than the rows available as a box at those rows, as for Overlay.

  • close_on_menu – close this dialog on a key for the menu command it leaves unhandled. None uses close_on_menu.

  • close_on_click_outside – close this dialog on a press of mouse button 1, 2 or 3 outside it. None uses close_on_click_outside.

  • on_close – called with the result when the dialog is closed, before "closed" is sent.

Raises:

  • ValueError – widget is already open in this stack. Also raised when align or valign is a string that names no alignment.

  • OverlayError – a layout option is not valid for Overlay.

sizing() → frozenset[Sizing]¶

Return box sizing, whatever is open.

class urwid.BarGraph(attlist: Sequence[str | tuple[str, str]], hatt: list[str] | None = None, satt: Mapping[tuple[int, int], str] | None = None)¶

Box widget that renders a bar graph from a sequence of data values.

Deprecated since version 4.0.10: Overriding get_data() in a subclass, or assigning get_data on an instance, is supported for backwards compatibility only. Call set_data() instead, so that the rendered canvas can be cached. This API will be removed in version 7.0.

Create a bar graph with the passed display characteristics.

See set_segment_attributes() for a description of the parameters.

calculate_bar_widths(size: tuple[int, int], bardata: Sequence[Sequence[float | int]]) → list[int]¶

If self.bar_width is None this implementation will stretch the bars across the available space specified by maxcol.

Calculate display data.

hlines_display(disp: list[tuple[int, list[tuple[int | tuple[int, int] | tuple[int, int, int], int]]]], top: float, hlines: Sequence[float | int], maxrow: int) → list[tuple[int, list[tuple[int | tuple[int, int] | tuple[int, int, int], int]]]]¶

Add hlines to display structure represented as bar_type tuple values.

The tuple is (bg, 0-5) where bg is the segment that has the hline on it, and 0-5 is the hline graphic to use where 0 is a regular underscore and 1-5 are the UTF-8 horizontal scan line characters.

Render BarGraph.

Raises:

BarGraphError – a graph character does not render as a single row.

selectable() → Literal[False]¶

Return False.

set_bar_width(width: int | None) → None¶

Set a preferred bar width for calculate_bar_widths to use.

Parameters:

width – width of bar or None for automatic width adjustment

Raises:

ValueError – width is not positive.

set_data(bardata: Sequence[Sequence[float | int]], top: float, hlines: Sequence[float | int] | None = None) → None¶

Store bar data, bargraph top and horizontal line positions.

Parameters:

  • bardata – a list of bar values.

  • top – maximum value for segments within bardata

  • hlines – None or a bar value marking horizontal line positions

bar values are [ segment1, segment2, … ] lists where top is the maximal value corresponding to the top of the bar graph and segment1, segment2, … are the values for the top of each segment of this bar. Simple bar graphs will only have one segment in each bar value.

Eg: if top is 100 and there is a bar value of [ 80, 30 ] then the top of this bar will be at 80% of full height of the graph and it will have a second segment that starts at 30%.

set_segment_attributes(attlist: Sequence[str | tuple[str, str]], hatt: list[str] | None = None, satt: Mapping[tuple[int, int], str] | None = None) → None¶

Set the display attributes to use for the bar graph’s segments.

Parameters:

  • attlist – list containing display attribute or (display attribute, character) tuple for background, first segment, and optionally following segments. ie. len(attlist) == num segments+1 character defaults to ‘ ‘ if not specified.

  • hatt – list containing attributes for horizontal lines. First element is for lines on background, second is for lines on first segment, third is for lines on second segment etc.

  • satt – dictionary containing attributes for smoothed transitions of bars in UTF-8 display mode. The values are in the form:

Raises:

BarGraphError –

attlist has fewer than two entries, or satt is not a mapping of valid (fg, bg) index pairs with fg above bg.

(fg,bg) : attr

fg and bg are integers where 0 is the graph background, 1 is the first segment, 2 is the second, … fg > bg in all values. attr is an attribute with a foreground corresponding to fg and a background corresponding to bg.

If satt is not None and the bar graph is being displayed in a terminal using the UTF-8 encoding then the character cell that is shared between the segments specified will be smoothed with using the UTF-8 vertical eighth characters.

eg: set_segment_attributes( [‘no’, (‘unsure’,”?”), ‘yes’] ) will use the attribute ‘no’ for the background (the area from the top of the graph to the top of the bar), question marks with the attribute ‘unsure’ will be used for the topmost segment of the bar, and the attribute ‘yes’ will be used for the bottom segment of the bar.

smooth_display(disp: list[tuple[int, list[tuple[int, int]]]]) → list[tuple[int, list[tuple[int | tuple[int, int] | tuple[int, int, int], int]]]]¶

Smooth (col, row*8) display into (col, row) display using UTF vertical eighth characters.

The characters are represented as bar_type tuple values (fg, bg, 1-7) where fg is the lower segment, bg is the upper segment and 1-7 is the vertical eighth character to use.

Raises:

BarGraphError – the smoothed rows do not add up to the graph height.

use_smoothed() → bool¶

Return whether smoothed (sub-character resolution) rendering can be used.

ProgressBar¶

class urwid.ProgressBar(normal: Hashable, complete: Hashable, current: float = 0, done: int = 100, satt: Hashable = None)¶

Flow widget that displays a completion percentage as a bar of Unicode block characters.

Build the progress bar with the given display attributes and range.

Parameters:

  • normal – display attribute for incomplete part of progress bar

  • complete – display attribute for complete part of progress bar

  • current – current progress

  • done – progress amount at 100%

  • satt – display attribute for smoothed part of bar where the foreground of satt corresponds to the normal part and the background corresponds to the complete part. Smoothing requires UTF-8 encoding. If satt is None then no smoothing will be done.

>>> from urwid import LineBox
>>> pb = ProgressBar("a", "b")
>>> pb
<ProgressBar flow widget>
>>> print(pb.get_text())
0 %
>>> pb.set_completion(34.42)
>>> print(pb.get_text())
34 %
>>> class CustomProgressBar(ProgressBar):
...     def get_text(self):
...         return "Foobar"
>>> cpb = CustomProgressBar("a", "b")
>>> print(cpb.get_text())
Foobar
>>> for x in range(101):
...     cpb.set_completion(x)
...     s = cpb.render((10,))
>>> cpb2 = CustomProgressBar("a", "b", satt="c")
>>> for x in range(101):
...     cpb2.set_completion(x)
...     s = cpb2.render((10,))
>>> pb = ProgressBar("a", "b", satt="c")
>>> pb.set_completion(34.56)
>>> print(LineBox(pb).render((20,)))
┌──────────────────┐
│      ▏34 %       │
└──────────────────┘

Spinner¶

class urwid.Spinner(frames: SpinnerFrames | Sequence[str] = SpinnerFrames.LINE, *, interval: float = 0.1, idle: _TagMarkup | None = None, loop: MainLoop | None = None, align: Literal['left', 'center', 'right'] | Align = Align.LEFT, wrap: Literal['space', 'any', 'clip', 'ellipsis'] | WrapMode = WrapMode.SPACE)¶

A text widget showing its frames in turn while some work runs.

start() shows the first frame and sets an alarm that shows the next one every interval seconds. The frame is chosen from the time elapsed since start(), so a late alarm skips frames instead of slowing the spinner down. stop() removes the alarm and shows the idle text, which is also shown before the first frame. step() shows the next frame by hand, for an application that drives the spinner from its own tick.

start(), step() and stop() replace the text, so put a label in its own Text next to the spinner, for example in a Columns. Every frame and the default idle text have one width, so a "pack" cell keeps its width.

The alarm is set on loop, or, without one, on the MainLoop running when start() is called (see get_running_loop()). The pending alarm keeps a running spinner alive: stop a spinner that leaves the screen.

Important

Call every method from the thread running the loop, like every other widget change. Another thread hands the call over with MainLoop.call_from_thread().

>>> spinner = Spinner(Spinner.Frames.LINE)
>>> spinner.render((3,)).text
[b'   ']
>>> spinner.step()
>>> spinner.render((3,)).text
[b'-  ']
>>> spinner.step()
>>> spinner.render((3,)).text
[b'\\  ']
>>> spinner.stop()
>>> spinner.render((3,)).text
[b'   ']

Build a stopped spinner showing the idle text.

Parameters:

  • frames – frames shown in turn, a Spinner.Frames member or a sequence of strings. Frames narrower than the widest are padded with spaces on the right.

  • interval – seconds each frame is shown while running, see interval.

  • idle – text markup shown while stopped, see idle.

  • loop – loop the alarm is set on. None uses the loop running at each start().

  • align – alignment of the text.

  • wrap – wrap mode of the text.

Raises:

  • TypeError – frames is not a Spinner.Frames member or a sequence of strings, or interval is not a number.

  • ValueError – frames is empty, a frame is not printable or is zero columns wide, or interval is not finite and > 0.

  • TextError – align or wrap is not supported by the text layout.

  • TagMarkupException – idle is not valid text markup.

Frames¶

alias of SpinnerFrames

property frames: tuple[str, ...]¶

The frames shown in turn, each padded to one width.

property idle: _TagMarkup | None¶

Text markup shown while stopped, or None for spaces as wide as a frame.

A new value shows at once while the idle text shows, and otherwise from the next stop().

Raises:

TagMarkupException – the new value is not valid text markup.

property interval: float¶

Seconds each frame is shown while running.

A new value applies at once: a running spinner keeps the frame showing and shows the next one after the new interval.

Raises:

  • TypeError – the new value is not a number.

  • ValueError – the new value is not finite and > 0.

  • Exception – the loop failed to set the new alarm; the spinner is then stopped.

property loop: MainLoop | None¶

Loop the alarm is set on, or None to use the loop running at each start().

property running: bool¶

Whether the frames are changing on an alarm, between start() and stop().

start() → None¶

Show frames in turn on an alarm, until stop().

A spinner started from the idle text shows the first frame. One started after step() goes on from the frame showing. A running spinner is left as it is. A call that raises leaves the spinner as it was.

Raises:

RuntimeError – there is no loop and no loop is running. Pass loop= to start a spinner before the loop runs.

step() → None¶

Show the next frame.

On a stopped spinner the first call shows the first frame. On a running one the frames after it keep the shift by one.

stop() → None¶

Remove the alarm and show the idle text.

A later start() begins at the first frame. A stopped spinner only shows the idle text again.

class urwid.widget.spinner.SpinnerFrames(*values)¶

Common frame sets for Spinner, also reachable as Spinner.Frames.

The frames of each member have one width. On a terminal without UTF-8:

  • LINE and DOTS are ASCII and are drawn as they are.

  • Every other member is drawn as its set_ascii_fallbacks() replacement, or as ? without one.

Note

The default terminal fonts of GNOME, KDE Plasma and Xfce on Ubuntu, Fedora and Arch, and of Windows Terminal, show every member. The default fonts of the Linux virtual console are:

  • Ubuntu: Fixed 8x16.

  • Fedora and openSUSE: eurlatgr.

  • Arch: the built-in 8x16 font of the kernel.

The default fonts of the Linux virtual console and of the classic Windows console show none of the non-ASCII members, so use LINE or DOTS there unless the console font has wider coverage.

Terminal¶

class urwid.Terminal(command: tuple[str | bytes | os.PathLike[str] | os.PathLike[bytes], ...] | list[str | bytes | os.PathLike[str] | os.PathLike[bytes]] | Callable[[], Any] | None, env: Mapping[str, str] | Iterable[tuple[str, str]] | None = None, main_loop: _WatchLoop | None = None, escape_sequence: str | None = None, encoding: str = 'utf-8')¶

Widget that runs a child process (or callable) and renders its terminal output.

Initialize a terminal emulator widget.

command is the command to execute inside the terminal, provided as a list of the command followed by its arguments. If ‘command’ is None, the command is the current user’s shell. You can also provide a callable instead of a command, which will be executed in the subprocess.

env can be used to pass custom environment variables. If omitted, os.environ is used.

main_loop is the loop to watch the pty on: an event loop or a MainLoop, whose remove_watch_file must accept the handle its watch_file returned. Left out, the terminal watches the pty on the started MainLoop it is rendered under, and while none runs it reads the pty on every render. The watch moves at the first render under another loop, or under no loop, and is removed by terminate().

escape_sequence is the urwid key symbol which should be used to break out of the terminal widget. If it’s not specified, ctrl a is used.

encoding specifies the encoding that is being used when local keypresses in Unicode are encoded into raw bytes. UTF-8 is used by default. Set this to the encoding of your terminal if you need to transmit characters to the spawned process in non-UTF8 encoding. Applies to Python 3.x only.

Note

If you notice your Terminal instance is not printing unicode glyphs correctly, make sure the global encoding for urwid is set to utf8 with urwid.set_encoding("utf8"). See Encodings Supported for more details.

add_watch() → None¶

Register the pty with a loop, so feed() runs on new child output.

The loop is main_loop, or without one the started MainLoop running in the caller’s context. Nothing is registered while a watch is set, or when there is no such loop.

beep() → None¶

Emit a “beep” signal for anything listening on this widget.

change_focus(has_focus: bool) → None¶

Ignore SIGINT if this widget has focus.

feed() → None¶

Read pending output from the pty and feed it to the terminal, terminating the child on EOF.

flush_responses() → None¶

Write every buffered response to the pty and clear the buffer.

get_cursor_coords(size: tuple[int, int]) → tuple[int, int] | None¶

Return the cursor coordinates for this terminal.

keypress(size: tuple[int, int], key: str) → str | None¶

Translate key into the byte sequence the child process expects and write it to the pty.

Returns:

None when the widget used key, or key when it did not: the child has exited, the key is handed down to the parent outside a key grab, or the linux terminal type the child is given has no byte form for it, as for a cursor or function key with shift, meta or ctrl.

leds(which: Literal['clear', 'scroll_lock', 'num_lock', 'caps_lock']) → None¶

Emit a “leds” signal asking the display to set keyboard LED state which.

mouse_event(size: tuple[int, int], event: str, button: int, col: int, row: int, focus: bool) → bool | None¶

Report a mouse event to the child in the tracking mode and the encoding the child turned on.

The report bytes are the ones xterm sends for the same event.

Returns:

True when the child tracks the mouse, also for an event its tracking mode does not report. Such events are a drag under mode 1000, the release of a wheel button, and under X10 compatibility mode (9) anything but a press of buttons 1 to 3. False when the event is left to the parent, in these cases:

  • the child has exited;

  • the child does not track the mouse, or tracks it in highlight mode (1001), which is not implemented;

  • the view is scrolled back from the screen the child sees;

  • the event is not a press, a release or a drag.

remove_watch() → None¶

Unregister the pty from the loop add_watch() registered it on, when it did.

render(size: tuple[int, int], focus: bool = False) → TermCanvas¶

Resize the terminal to size, read any pending child output, and return the terminal canvas.

respond(string: str) → None¶

Respond to the underlying application with ‘string’.

set_termsize(width: int, height: int) → None¶

Tell the pty the terminal window is now width by height characters.

set_title(title: str) → None¶

Emit a “title” signal with the terminal’s new title.

spawn() → None¶

Fork the child process running command and connect it to a new pty.

terminate() → None¶

Stop watching the pty, end the child process and close the pty master.

Signals escalate from SIGHUP to SIGKILL until the child exits. A child that may not be signalled, such as a setuid program, only gets the hangup from closing the master. It is then waited for at most one second, and left unreaped if it keeps running.

touch_term(width: int, height: int) → None¶

Spawn the child process if needed, then resize the pty and terminal canvas to width by height.

wait_and_feed(timeout: float = 1.0) → None¶

Block up to timeout seconds for pty output, then read and process whatever has arrived.

Scroll Widget Classes¶

Scrollable¶

class urwid.Scrollable(widget: WrappedScrollWidget, force_forward_keypress: bool = False, *, delegate_selectable: bool = False)¶

Box widget decoration that makes a fixed or flow widget vertically scrollable.

Box widget that makes a fixed or flow widget vertically scrollable.

Note

Focusable widgets are handled, including switching focus, but possibly not intuitively, depending on the arrangement of widgets.

When switching focus to a widget that is ouside of the visible part of the original widget, the canvas scrolls up/down to the focused widget.

It would be better to scroll until the next focusable widget is in sight first. But for that to work we must somehow obtain a list of focusable rows in the original canvas.

Parameters:

  • widget – fixed or flow widget to scroll.

  • force_forward_keypress – pass every key to widget first, even when it shows no cursor.

  • delegate_selectable – take the input focus only when widget is selectable. A widget that is not, such as a Text, then cannot be scrolled by keys.

Raises:

ValueError – widget is neither a FIXED nor a FLOW widget.

get_scrollpos(size: tuple[int, int] | None = None, focus: bool = False) → int¶

Return the current scrolling position.

Lower limit is 0, upper limit is the maximum number of rows with the given maxcol minus maxrow.

..note::

The returned value may be too low or too high if the position has changed but the widget wasn’t rendered yet.

keypress(size: tuple[int, int], key: str) → str | None¶

Handle scrolling keys, forwarding everything else to the wrapped widget when appropriate.

mouse_event(size: tuple[int, int], event: str, button: int, col: int, row: int, focus: bool) → bool | None¶

Forward a mouse event to the wrapped widget, adjusting the row for the current scroll position.

render(size: tuple[int, int], focus: bool = False) → CompositeCanvas¶

Render the wrapped widget, trimmed to the current scroll position.

rows_max(size: tuple[int, int] | None = None, focus: bool = False) → int¶

Return the number of rows for size.

If size is not given, the currently rendered number of rows is returned.

Raises:

ScrollableError – the wrapped widget is neither a FLOW nor a FIXED widget.

selectable() → bool¶

Return whether the widget accepts the input focus.

Always True, unless delegate_selectable is set: then what the wrapped widget returns.

set_scrollpos(position: SupportsInt) → None¶

Set scrolling position.

If position is positive it is interpreted as lines from the top. If position is negative it is interpreted as lines from the bottom.

Values that are too high or too low values are automatically adjusted during rendering.

sizing() → frozenset[Sizing]¶

Return that this widget is always a box widget.

ScrollBar¶

class urwid.ScrollBar(widget: WrappedScrollableWidget, thumb_char: str = ScrollbarSymbols.FULL_BLOCK, trough_char: str = ' ', side: Literal['left', 'right'] = 'right', width: int = 1, *, visible: bool | None = None, scroll_by_focus: bool = False, delegate_selectable: bool = False, end_markers: tuple[str, str] | None = None, attr: Hashable = None, focus_attr: Hashable = None, thumb_attr: Hashable = None, thumb_focus_attr: Hashable = None, marker_dim_attr: Hashable = None)¶

Widget decoration that adds a scrollbar alongside a scrollable wrapped widget.

Create a widget that adds a scrollbar to widget.

Parameters:

  • widget –

    box widget that has, or wraps a widget that has, the following methods:

    • get_scrollpos takes the arguments size and focus and returns the index of the first visible row.

    • set_scrollpos (optional, on the same widget as get_scrollpos; needed for mouse click and drag support on the scrollbar) takes the index of the first visible row. The scrollbar does not use ListBox.set_scrollpos(); see scroll_by_focus instead.

    • rows_max takes size and focus and returns the total number of rows widget can render.

  • thumb_char – character used for the scrollbar handle.

  • trough_char – character used for the space above and below the handle.

  • side – side the scrollbar is drawn on, 'left' or 'right'.

  • width – number of columns the scrollbar uses, at least 1.

  • visible – when the scrollbar is drawn: None draws it only when widget needs scrolling, True always, so the wrapped widget always gets the same width, and False never, so the wrapped widget gets the full width and is still scrolled by keys and wheel.

  • scroll_by_focus – let a click or drag on the scrollbar scroll a ListBox by moving its focus to the widget at the top of the new view. The focus then changes without passing through the ListBox keypress or mouse_event, so this is off by default for code that tracks the focus there.

  • delegate_selectable – take the input focus only when widget is selectable; a ListBox created with focus_when_empty=False is not while it is empty. Off by default, so a wrapped widget that is not selectable can still be scrolled by keys.

  • end_markers – characters drawn in the first and the last scrollbar row, or None for no markers, such as (ScrollBar.Symbols.ARROW_TRIANGLE_UP, ScrollBar.Symbols.ARROW_TRIANGLE_DOWN). They are drawn only when the scrollbar has at least 4 rows, so the thumb has 2 trough rows to move in, and a click on one scrolls one step towards its end, as the mouse wheel does.

  • attr – display attribute of the trough and the end markers.

  • focus_attr – display attribute of the trough and the end markers when rendered in focus; None uses attr.

  • thumb_attr – display attribute of the thumb; None uses attr.

  • thumb_focus_attr – display attribute of the thumb when rendered in focus; None uses thumb_attr when it is set, and focus_attr otherwise.

  • marker_dim_attr – display attribute of an end marker whose end of the content is visible; None draws it like the other marker. An end counts as visible only when the first or last row of the content is on screen. A custom widget scrolled by items rather than rows, through SupportsRelativeScroll, cannot report cut-off rows, so for it an end counts once its first or last item is on screen.

Raises:

  • ValueError – widget is not a BOX widget, or end_markers is not a pair.

  • TypeError – widget does not wrap anything that supports the scrolling protocol.

Symbols¶

alias of ScrollbarSymbols

get_cursor_coords(size: tuple[int] | tuple[int, int]) → tuple[int, int] | None¶

Return the cursor of the wrapped widget, moved past the scrollbar columns when they are on the left.

Returns:

None when the wrapped widget has no get_cursor_coords or no cursor.

keypress(size: tuple[int] | tuple[int, int], key: str) → str | None¶

Forward a keypress to the wrapped widget, at the size it is rendered at within size.

mouse_event(size: tuple[int] | tuple[int, int], event: str, button: int, col: int, row: int, focus: bool) → bool | None¶

Handle a mouse event, dispatching it to the scrollbar thumb/trough or to the wrapped widget.

A press of button 1 on the scrollbar, and the drag that follows it, move the thumb top to the pointer row. So does its release on displays that report the button of a release, such as curses, which send no drags. A press of button 1 on an end marker scrolls one step towards that end, as the mouse wheel does, and the drag and release that follow it do nothing. Events in the wrapped widget’s columns go to it. On the scrollbar, the vertical mouse wheel of a widget the scrollbar does not scroll through set_scrollpos (such as ListBox) is passed on, together with the drags and releases described below; other events there are not.

A drag or release goes where its press went: a drag started on the scrollbar keeps moving the thumb over the wrapped widget’s columns, and a drag started on the wrapped widget stays with it over the scrollbar. A drag or release whose press was not seen here, such as the end of a drag and drop started in another widget, goes to the wrapped widget. Events outside this widget never reach it, so a release there is not seen; the next press here starts over.

render(size: tuple[int] | tuple[int, int], focus: bool = False) → Canvas¶

Render the wrapped widget together with the scrollbar, when scrolling is needed.

A flow size renders the wrapped widget at its flow rows, so it never needs scrolling.

rows(size: tuple[int], focus: bool = False) → int¶

Return the rows of the wrapped widget at the width it is rendered at.

With visible True the scrollbar always takes its columns, so the wrapped widget gets the rest.

Raises:

AttributeError – the wrapped widget has no rows(), as a Scrollable has none.

property scroll_by_focus: bool¶

Whether a click or drag on the scrollbar scrolls a ListBox by moving its focus.

property scrollbar_side: Literal['left', 'right']¶

Where to display the scrollbar; must be ‘left’ or ‘right’.

property scrollbar_width: int¶

Columns the scrollbar uses.

property scrolling_base_widget: SupportsScroll¶

Nearest original_widget that is compatible with the scrolling API.

Raises:

ScrollableError – no wrapped widget supports the scrolling protocol.

selectable() → bool¶

Return whether the widget accepts the input focus.

Always True, unless delegate_selectable is set: then what the wrapped widget returns.

sizing() → frozenset[Sizing]¶

Return BOX, and FLOW as well for a wrapped ListBox with ListBox.flow set.

The ListBox may be wrapped in decorations such as AttrMap, as long as they report FLOW too.

property visible: bool | None¶

When the scrollbar is drawn: None when scrolling is needed, True always, False never.

class urwid.widget.scrollable.ScrollbarSymbols(*values)¶

Common symbols suitable for scrollbar.

The thumb and trough symbols come first, and the ARROW_* pairs for the end markers follow them.

Only these members are also drawn on terminals without UTF-8, where the others are drawn as ?:

  • ASCII: ARROW_ASCII_UP and ARROW_ASCII_DOWN.

  • DEC special graphics: MEDIUM_SHADE, DRAWING_LIGHT, BLACK_VERTICAL_RECTANGLE and MIDDLE_DOT.

Note

The default terminal fonts of GNOME, KDE Plasma and Xfce on Ubuntu, Fedora and Arch, and of Windows Terminal, show every member. The default fonts of the Linux virtual console are:

  • Ubuntu: Fixed 8x16.

  • Fedora and openSUSE: eurlatgr.

  • Arch: the built-in 8x16 font of the kernel.

The default fonts of the Linux virtual console and of the classic Windows console show these non-ASCII members:
